content: If a woman is amenorrheic, a copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD) can be inserted at any time, provided it is confirmed that she is not pregnant. When using ulipristal acetate (UPA) for emergency contraception, the woman should abstain from sexual intercourse or use barrier contraception until her new contraceptive method becomes effective. For progestogen-only pills (POPs), this requires an additional two days, while for other hormonal methods, an additional seven days is necessary. If a Cu-IUD is inserted, no additional contraceptive protection or abstinence is required. UPA, an anti-progestogen, may interact with progestogen-containing contraceptive methods, potentially reducing the effectiveness of either drug. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) recommends starting a regular progestogen-containing method, including combined hormonal methods, on the sixth day after taking UPA to avoid drug interactions while sperm remain viable in the female genital tract following unprotected intercourse. If no withdrawal bleeding occurs within three weeks of taking UPA, pregnancy should be ruled out. The Cu-IUD is contraindicated during pregnancy due to the risk of severe pelvic infection and septic spontaneous abortion. For postpartum, non-breastfeeding women or non-postpartum amenorrheic women, the standard six criteria for determining non-pregnancy may not apply. Alternative methods should be used to confirm pregnancy status. The Standard Days Method (SDM), a fertility awareness-based method, is suitable for women with regular menstrual cycles lasting 26–32 days. Women should avoid unprotected intercourse on days 8–19 of their cycle. However, SDM may not be appropriate for women with medical conditions where pregnancy poses a high risk, as it has relatively higher failure rates with typical use. SDM does not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV, and consistent condom use is recommended for STI prevention. Male sterilization, or vasectomy, is a low-risk outpatient procedure involving occlusion of the vas deferens. It is considered a permanent contraceptive method, and men should wait three months post-procedure before relying on it for contraception. During this period, additional contraceptive methods should be used. Semen analysis, where available, can confirm the absence of sperm and the effectiveness of the vasectomy. Vasectomy does not protect against STIs, and condom use is recommended if there is a risk of STI/HIV exposure.
